1	Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over chain-of-thought traces saturates as sample count grows because same-model traces are correlated voters.
2	We investigate whether symbolic constraint extraction can break this plateau through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts first-order logic (FOL) constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT.
3	Evaluating six models (7B--32B) across three reasoning domains with over 3,000 instances, we find that self-extracted constraints fail to surpass majority voting: zero of nine conditions reaches $p < 0.05$, while multiple conditions show significant degradation.
4	We identify \emph{symbolic confirmation bias} as the root cause: on incorrect problems, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC.
5	Process-level analysis reveals a deeper bottleneck: chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level Fleiss' $\kappa$ ($0.41$), indicating that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on answers.
6	More than twenty remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions---all fail, revealing a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: methods that increase trace independence destroy accuracy (Debate: $\kappa = 0.15$, $-18.6$\,pp), while methods preserving accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three model families).
7	Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound ($+14.22$\,pp FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp ProofWriter, $p < 0.001$); self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling.
8	The bottleneck is structural at the 7B--32B scale and universal across architectures.

42	\label{sec:confirmation-bias}
43	
44	The correlation above manifests through a specific mechanism: self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer regardless of correctness. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), when SICA errs, 83.3\% of extracted constraints support the incorrect majority answer---a bias ratio of $4.97\times$ compared to correct problems. Consequently, 94\% of SICA errors overlap with SC errors: symbolic aggregation adds no independent corrective signal.
45	
46	The 12 instances where SICA corrects SC errors reveal the mechanism's boundary: 43\% of these flips occur when a minority trace provides gold-aligned constraints, suggesting constraint diversity---not MAX-SAT---drives the rare successes. The causal chain is: the model generates an answer, then extracts FOL consistent with that answer; aggregation over such constraints reduces to a weighted majority vote (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}).
47	
48	Iterative refinement does not break this cycle. CEGIS achieves $\Delta = +3.43$\,pp in round~1 but oscillates in rounds~2--5 without convergence, as each step reintroduces model bias. Cross-model extraction (Qwen3-14B or Qwen2.5-14B extracting from Mistral-7B traces) produces accuracy within $\pm 1$\,pp of self-extraction---the bias is a property of LLM formalization itself. The oracle ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) confirms that 75.9\% of the potential gain is lost to self-extraction quality, localizing confirmation bias as the binding bottleneck.

51	\subsection{Process-Level Independence}
52	\label{sec:process-kappa}
53	
54	Answer-level $\kappa$ may underestimate the independence bottleneck: two traces can follow nearly identical reasoning yet reach different final answers, causing $\kappa$ to treat them as disagreeing. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), the mean pairwise cosine similarity of chain-of-thought traces (TF-IDF, Eq.~\ref{eq:process-sim}) is $0.69$, far exceeding answer-level $\kappa = 0.41$. These measures are uncorrelated ($r = -0.06$, $p = 0.36$): problems with diverse answers do not exhibit diverse reasoning. We find 9.3\% of trace pairs converge on reasoning ($\cos > 0.8$) while disagreeing on the final answer---apparent answer diversity masking process-level homogeneity.

+\label{sec:cross-arch-method}
+The oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) implies that external signal---not same-model refinement---is needed.
+As a proof-of-concept, we test whether a lightweight cross-architecture model can supply such signal.

+This 44M-parameter model shares no architecture, training data, or reasoning process with the 7B reasoning LLM, providing a genuinely independent signal.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:exp-setup}

We evaluate SICA against Self-Consistency (SC) across six models on three reasoning domains with over 3,000 instances. Beyond accuracy comparisons, we conduct diagnostic analyses of symbolic confirmation bias and process-level trace independence (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).

\paragraph{Models.} Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B (non-thinking mode)~\citep{yang2024qwen25}, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3~\citep{jiang2023mistral}, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct~\citep{dubey2024llama3}, and QwQ-32B~\citep{qwen2024qwq} (7B--32B parameters).

\paragraph{Datasets.} FOLIO~\citep{han2022folio} ($n{=}204$, with gold FOL annotations), ProofWriter depth-5~\citep{tafjord2021proofwriter} ($n{=}600$), LogiQA~\citep{liu2020logiqa} ($n{=}200$). StrategyQA~\citep{geva2021strategyqa} ($n{=}200$) serves as a domain-formalizability diagnostic. GSM8K~\citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} ($n{=}30$) and AIME 2024 ($n{=}22$) probe the degenerate regime ($C_0 < 5\%$).

\paragraph{Parameters.} $K{=}12$ traces at $T{=}0.7$; extraction at $T_{\text{ext}}{=}0.3$. Z3 timeout: 10s. $\alpha{=}0.5$. Statistical significance via McNemar exact test ($\alpha{=}0.05$); 95\% bootstrap CIs from 10,000 resamples for $n \geq 200$.


\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reports accuracy across all conditions sorted by SC baseline. SICA effectiveness depends sharply on the accuracy regime.

Failure modes detailed in Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrrl@{}}
\toprule
Model & Domain & $n$ & SC (\%) & SICA (\%) & $\Delta$ (pp) & $p$ \\
\midrule

Mistral-7B & PW-D5 & 600 & 39.33 & 36.50 & $\mathbf{-2.83}$ & 0.014{*} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{7}{l}{\textit{Intermediate SC (SC $\sim$50--55\%, Mistral-7B only)}} \\
Mistral-7B & LogiQA & 200 & 51.00 & 51.50 & $+$0.50 & 1.000 \\

\paragraph{Intermediate-SC region.} Mistral-7B on FOLIO (SC $\sim$50--55\%) shows positive directional trends in 2 of 4 seeds: $\Delta = +3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.092$) and $+2.94$\,pp ($p = 0.070$); the remaining seeds show null or negative results. \paragraph{Type A (SC $\geq$ 60\%): confirmation bias.} Nine conditions with SC $\geq 63\%$ (combined $N > 2{,}800$) produce no significant positive effects. Qwen2.5-14B on ProofWriter shows significant degradation ($\Delta = -2.50$\,pp, $p = 0.011$). Even in-context learning with gold FOL examples ($\Delta = +0.50$\,pp, n.s.) cannot break confirmation bias.

\paragraph{Type C (SC $\leq$ 40\%): error amplification.} Mistral-7B on ProofWriter ($n = 600$, SC $= 39.33\%$) shows $\Delta = -2.83$\,pp ($p = 0.014$): SICA \emph{significantly hurts} by formalizing incorrect reasoning.

\paragraph{Degenerate cases.} When $C_0 < 5\%$, nearly all traces agree and SICA reduces to SC by construction.

Figure~\ref{fig:regime-scatter} visualizes the regime dependence: the intermediate-SC region is narrow and observed only for Mistral-7B on FOLIO.

\caption{SICA $\Delta$ (pp) vs.\ SC baseline. Filled: $n \geq 100$; open: $n < 100$. The intermediate-SC region (50--55\%, shaded) contains the only positive trends (none reaching $p < 0.05$). Type~C: significant degradation ($p = 0.014$).}
\label{fig:regime-scatter}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Oracle Control}
\label{sec:oracle}

Oracle variants replace self-extracted constraints with gold annotations: FOL from FOLIO ($n = 204$) and DSL from ProofWriter ($n = 600$). Oracle-SICA achieves 89.71\% on FOLIO ($\Delta = +14.22$\,pp, $p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$) and 86.67\% on ProofWriter ($\Delta = +11.50$\,pp, $p = 9.21 \times 10^{-15}$). Z3 agrees with gold labels on 95.1\% (FOLIO) and 97.1\% (ProofWriter) of problems.

These results establish that the MAX-SAT mechanism is sound given discriminative constraints. Mistral-7B's best self-extracted result ($+3.43$\,pp) captures only 24.1\% of the FOLIO oracle ceiling. The remaining 75.9\% is lost to self-extraction quality.


\subsection{Four-Seed Replication}
\label{sec:replication}

Four seeds on Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$, $K = 12$, $T = 0.7$) yield $\Delta$ from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp (mean $+1.47$\,pp); 2 of 4 show marginal trends ($p < 0.10$), none reaches $p < 0.05$. Seeds~42 and~456 share identical SC baselines (55.88\%) yet diverge ($+3.43$ vs.\ $0.00$\,pp), indicating seed-level constraint quality---not SC level alone---drives the effect (entropy decomposition in Appendix~\ref{app:entropy}).

+\subsection{Cross-Architecture Verification}
+\label{sec:cross-arch}
+The oracle gap motivates testing whether external signal can help in practice.
+DeBERTa-v3-small NLI (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch-method}) provides a cross-architecture verification signal on Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$, seed~123).
+DeBERTa NLI alone achieves 49.51\% (below SC's 54.41\%), but the \emph{combo} mode (NLI + SC, $w{=}3$) reaches 57.84\% ($\Delta = +3.43$\,pp over SC).
+Per-label analysis reveals complementary strengths: NLI improves accuracy on \textsc{False} problems by $+33$\,pp over SC, while SC dominates on \textsc{Unknown} by $+49$\,pp.

+While preliminary (single seed, one dataset), the result provides proof-of-concept evidence that the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) is practically recoverable through cross-architecture verification, consistent with published systems that bypass self-extraction \citep{xu2026dylos, wang2025fover}.

lines: \label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{Symbolic confirmation bias as unifying root cause.}

-The oracle experiments causally identify the failure source: gold constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$) while self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}). Symbolic confirmation bias (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}) unifies the two channels through which trace correlation degrades SICA. The \emph{direct} channel limits voting diversity (Eff-$K < 2$ for many conditions); the \emph{indirect} channel operates through constraint quality, as correlated traces produce homogeneous constraints that cause MAX-SAT to degenerate to vote counting (Appendix~\ref{app:ablation}). Both stem from a single mechanism: the model generates an answer, then extracts FOL consistent with that answer. More than twenty remediation strategies fail because each addresses a symptom---diversity, filtering, alternative solvers---rather than this root cause.

The cross-architecture NLI experiment (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}) corroborates this diagnosis: a 44M-parameter DeBERTa model, sharing no architecture or training data with the reasoning LLM, provides the complementary signal that same-model methods cannot.
\paragraph{Process-level implications.}

The gap between process-level similarity ($0.69$) and answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$) implies that the independence bottleneck is deeper than answer-level metrics suggest (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}). Interventions that successfully spread answers across candidates may still fail to diversify the underlying reasoning, explaining why temperature scaling and diverse prompting produce no SICA improvement despite affecting answer distributions.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated SICA across six models (three families), three reasoning domains, and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication. The root cause of self-extraction failure is symbolic confirmation bias: on incorrect problems, 83.3\% of constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC. Process-level analysis reveals a deeper bottleneck: chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), indicating reasoning homogeneity beyond what answer distributions suggest. More than twenty remediation strategies all fail to escape the resulting independence-accuracy Pareto frontier ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three families). Oracle controls confirm the mechanism is sound ($+14.22$\,pp FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp ProofWriter); self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling. For practitioners, $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated SICA across six models (three families), three reasoning domains, and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication. The root cause of self-extraction failure is symbolic confirmation bias: on incorrect problems, 83.3\% of constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC. Process-level analysis reveals a deeper bottleneck: chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), indicating reasoning homogeneity beyond what answer distributions suggest. More than twenty remediation strategies all fail to escape the resulting independence-accuracy Pareto frontier ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three families). We investigate whether symbolic constraint extraction can break this plateau through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts first-order logic (FOL) constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT.

Process-level analysis reveals a deeper bottleneck: chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level Fleiss' $\kappa$ ($0.41$), indicating that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on answers.
More than twenty remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions---all fail, revealing a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: methods that increase trace independence destroy accuracy (Debate: $\kappa = 0.15$, $-18.6$\,pp), while methods preserving accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three model families).
Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound ($+14.22$\,pp FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp ProofWriter, $p < 0.001$); self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling.

24	We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).

26

28	The central finding is a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
29	Whether larger models or trained extractors can overcome this remains open.
30	
31	Our contributions are:
32	\begin{enumerate}
33	\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ generalization across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a Pareto frontier: methods that increase independence destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). 34	
35	\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} Self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer: bias ratio $4.97\times$ on incorrect problems, 94\% error overlap with SC. The causal chain---model generates answer, extracts consistent FOL, Z3 aggregation mirrors majority vote---explains why self-extraction cannot correct errors the model has already committed (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
36	
37	\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence Quantification.} Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), establishing that reasoning processes are more homogeneous than answer distributions suggest. 38	
39	\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Pattern and Diagnostics.} Three failure modes---confirmation bias (SC $\geq 60\%$), non-formalizability, error amplification (SC $\leq 40\%$)---create regime boundaries. $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost diagnostic predicting when symbolic augmentation is unlikely to help (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
40	\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch: same-model traces carry correlated errors, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct shared bias.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
Recent neuro-symbolic methods---Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm}, LINC \citep{olausson2023linc}, DyLoS \citep{xu2026dylos}, Aristotle \citep{li2025aristotle}, FoVer \citep{wang2025fover}, LogicAgent \citep{luo2025logicagent}---each report gains on logical reasoning, but introduce components beyond the reasoning model: trained verifiers, solver selection, or external knowledge.
A simpler question precedes these: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
Self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model, training data, or external prover.
Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation.

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.

We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
More than twenty remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions targeting the independence bottleneck---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is structural at the 7B--32B scale tested.

Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL yields $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
The central finding is a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
Whether larger models or trained extractors can overcome this remains open.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ generalization across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a Pareto frontier: methods that increase independence destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). More than twenty remediation strategies all fail (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} Self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer: bias ratio $4.97\times$ on incorrect problems, 94\% error overlap with SC. The causal chain---model generates answer, extracts consistent FOL, Z3 aggregation mirrors majority vote---explains why self-extraction cannot correct errors the model has already committed (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence Quantification.} Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), establishing that reasoning processes are more homogeneous than answer distributions suggest. Combined with Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across 15 conditions and three model families, this quantifies the independence ceiling for same-model trace aggregation (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}, \S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Pattern and Diagnostics.} Three failure modes---confirmation bias (SC $\geq 60\%$), non-formalizability, error amplification (SC $\leq 40\%$)---create regime boundaries. $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost diagnostic predicting when symbolic augmentation is unlikely to help (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch: same-model traces carry correlated errors, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct shared bias.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
Recent neuro-symbolic methods---Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm}, LINC \citep{olausson2023linc}, DyLoS \citep{xu2026dylos}, Aristotle \citep{li2025aristotle}, FoVer \citep{wang2025fover}, LogicAgent \citep{luo2025logicagent}---each report gains on logical reasoning, but introduce components beyond the reasoning model: trained verifiers, solver selection, or external knowledge.
A simpler question precedes these: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
Self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model, training data, or external prover.
Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation.

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.

We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
More than twenty-five remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions targeting the independence bottleneck---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is structural at the 7B--32B scale tested.

Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL yields $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
The central finding is a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
A cross-architecture proof-of-concept demonstrates that this gap is recoverable: DeBERTa-small NLI combined with SC achieves $+3.43$\,pp through per-label complementarity (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ generalization across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a Pareto frontier: methods that increase independence destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). More than twenty remediation strategies all fail (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} Self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer: bias ratio $4.97\times$ on incorrect problems, 94\% error overlap with SC. The causal chain---model generates answer, extracts consistent FOL, Z3 aggregation mirrors majority vote---explains why self-extraction cannot correct errors the model has already committed (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence Quantification.} Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), establishing that reasoning processes are more homogeneous than answer distributions suggest. Combined with Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across 15 conditions and three model families, this quantifies the independence ceiling for same-model trace aggregation (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}, \S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Pattern and Diagnostics.} Three failure modes---confirmation bias (SC $\geq 60\%$), non-formalizability, error amplification (SC $\leq 40\%$)---create regime boundaries. $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost diagnostic predicting when symbolic augmentation is unlikely to help (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
\end{enumerate}

content.content: 1	Our evaluation covers same-model self-extraction and cross-model extraction in both directions (\S\ref{sec:remediation}), but we do not test trained FOL extractors or external solvers with verified grounding, which may overcome the independence bottleneck. The intermediate-SC region where positive trends occur is narrow (SC $\approx$ 50--55\%) and observed in only one model-dataset condition, limiting practical applicability. All models range from 7B to 32B; whether the bottleneck persists at larger scales (70B+) remains untested. The oracle analysis covers two formal logic benchmarks with gold annotations (FOLIO, ProofWriter); extending to commonsense or open-domain reasoning requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets. Four-seed replication shows effects ranging from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp, with 2 of 4 seeds yielding null or negative results. The optimal $K$ and temperature settings cannot be determined without labeled data (Appendix~\ref{app:sensitivity}). All evaluation datasets are English-language logical reasoning benchmarks with discrete answer spaces (binary or multiple-choice); whether confirmation bias generalizes to open-ended generation or multilingual settings is untested. The process-level independence metric (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}) uses TF-IDF representations, which may underweight semantic similarity not captured by lexical overlap. Additional limitations regarding power analysis, prompt templates, and deduplication strategy are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:limitations-extended}.

+\paragraph{Scope of evaluation.}

+Our evaluation covers same-model self-extraction and cross-model extraction in both directions (\S\ref{sec:remediation}), but we do not test trained FOL extractors or external solvers with verified grounding. All models range from 7B to 32B; whether the bottleneck persists at larger scales (70B+) remains untested. All evaluation datasets are English-language logical reasoning benchmarks with discrete answer spaces (binary or multiple-choice); whether confirmation bias generalizes to open-ended generation or multilingual settings is untested. The oracle analysis covers two formal logic benchmarks with gold annotations (FOLIO, ProofWriter); extending to commonsense or open-domain reasoning requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets.
+\paragraph{Statistical and methodological caveats.}

+The symbolic confirmation bias metric (bias ratio $4.97\times$) is computed on a single condition (Mistral-7B FOLIO, $n = 204$); generalizability across models and domains requires further validation. Four-seed replication shows effects ranging from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp, with 2 of 4 seeds yielding null or negative results. The intermediate-SC region where positive trends occur is narrow (SC $\approx$ 50--55\%) and observed in only one model-dataset condition. The process-level independence metric (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}) uses TF-IDF representations, which may underweight semantic similarity not captured by lexical overlap. The cross-architecture NLI result (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}) is preliminary: single seed, single dataset, without McNemar significance testing.
+\paragraph{Computational cost and sensitivity.}

+SICA imposes ${\sim}$49\% wall-time overhead over SC due to constraint extraction (Appendix~\ref{app:sensitivity}). The extraction prompt uses a single zero-shot template per domain; alternative prompting strategies (few-shot, chain-of-thought extraction) might yield different results, though the oracle gap suggests the bottleneck is fundamental. The optimal $K$ and temperature settings cannot be determined without labeled data. Additional limitations regarding power analysis and deduplication strategy are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:limitations-extended}.
